Washington property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • Petition to the county board of equalization must be filed on or before July 1st of the year of the assessment, or within a time limit of up to 60 days adopted by the county legislative authority, whichever is later. (RCW 84.40.038; source)
  • The board of equalization may waive the filing deadline for good cause if the petition is filed within a reasonable time after the deadline. (RCW 84.40.038; source)
  • An appeal may go directly to the state board of tax appeals if the assessor, the owner, and a majority of the county board of equalization agree. (RCW 84.40.038; source)
  • All property must be valued at 100 percent of its true and fair value in money and assessed on the same basis unless specifically provided otherwise by law. (RCW 84.40.030; source)
  • After three years from the date of delinquency, the county treasurer issues certificates of delinquency and proceeds to foreclose the tax liens in the county's name. (RCW 84.64.050; source)
  • After judgment, the county treasurer sells the property to the highest bidder; minimum bid is total taxes, interest and costs; property is sold 'as is'. (RCW 84.64.080; source)

How is property tax set in Washington?

Each county assessor values every parcel once a year, and each county treasurer collects the bill. Under RCW 84.40.020, real property is listed and assessed every year with reference to its value on January 1 of that year.

The standard of value is set by RCW 84.40.030: property is valued at 100 percent of its true and fair value in money. For a house, the assessor looks first at sales of the property or similar properties made within the past five years. The assessor must also respect existing zoning, so a value cannot be built on a use the land is not allowed to have. Land and structures are valued separately, and the two cannot add up to more than the property is worth as it stands.

When the assessor changes your value, a notice must go out no later than thirty days after the appraisal (RCW 84.40.045). It shows the old and new value, land and improvements listed separately, plus a short description of how to appeal. No such notice may be mailed between January 15 and February 15.

When are Washington property taxes due?

Washington taxes are due in two halves: the first on or before April 30 and the second on or before October 31. RCW 84.56.020 sets the calendar, and the half-and-half option applies when the tax on a parcel is $50 or more.

ItemWhat the statute says
First halfDue on or before April 30
Second halfDue on or before October 31
Tax statementsDistributed by March 15 when budgets, levies and the tax roll are delivered on schedule
Interest, residential parcel with four or fewer units9 percent per year, computed monthly from delinquency, with no penalty
Interest, other property12 percent per year
Penalties on nonresidential, larger multifamily and personal property3 percent on tax delinquent June 1, plus 8 percent more on December 1

Source: RCW 84.56.020 (app.leg.wa.gov).

Payments sent by mail without a readable postmark, and payments from an automated check service, count as on time if they arrive within three business days of the due date. Treasurers may also offer payment agreements and accept partial payments, applied to the oldest delinquent year first unless you ask otherwise. Ask your county treasurer which options it runs.

How do I appeal a Washington property assessment?

File a petition with your county board of equalization on the state form. RCW 84.40.038 gives you whichever is latest of these deadlines:

  • July 1 of the year of the assessment.
  • Thirty days after the assessment or value change notice was mailed.
  • Thirty days after the assessor sent it electronically or told you it was available online.
  • A county-adopted window of up to sixty days.

A petition that is not on the prescribed form or not fully completed may be refused, so read the form before you send it. If you miss the date, the board may waive it when you file within a reasonable time and show good cause. The statute lists examples: a death or serious illness in the family, being away from your mailing address for more than fifteen of the allowed days when the deadline falls after July 1, wrong written advice from county staff, a flood or earthquake, or a postal delay the post office has documented. The board must waive the deadline if you were never sent a revaluation notice even though your area was revalued and your value did not change.

You and the assessor can also ask for a direct appeal to the state Board of Tax Appeals if the assessor, you, and a majority of the county board all agree. The state board may decline, and the county board then hears the case. The Board of Tax Appeals publishes appeal forms and a checklist for residential owners who want to go further than the county board.

If a bill comes due while your appeal is still open, ask the county treasurer how to handle the payment.

What tax relief can Washington homeowners get?

The main programs are an exemption, a deferral, and a grant for certain widows and widowers of veterans. The Department of Revenue describes each on its exemptions and deferrals page, and your county assessor takes the applications.

  • Senior, disability and veteran exemption. You must own and occupy your primary residence in Washington and have income at or below your county's threshold. You must also be at least 61 by December 31 of the assessment year, unable to work because of a disability, or a veteran with a qualifying VA rating. The reduction depends on income, home value and local levy rates, and renewal is required at least once every six years as the assessor decides.
  • Senior and disability deferral. Available to owner-occupants who are 60 or older, or retired because of disability, with enough equity to secure the state's interest. Deferred tax accrues 5 percent simple interest and must be repaid when the home is sold, the owner dies, or the home stops being the primary residence.
  • Widow or widower of a veteran. A grant that does not have to be repaid if the recipient lives in the home until at least December 15 of the year it is received.

Two related protections sit in the collection statutes. A treasurer may not sell a property that is eligible for deferral and instead must require the owner to file a declaration to defer (RCW 84.64.050(6)). And under RCW 84.56.020(19), an income-qualified owner who lives in a home already facing tax foreclosure can have outstanding interest and penalties waived once, starting about 60 days before the three-year mark.

Income limits differ by county. Ask your county assessor for the current threshold for your county before you decide whether to apply.

What happens when property taxes go unpaid in Washington?

Interest runs from the date of delinquency, and after three years the county moves toward foreclosure. RCW 84.64.050 directs the treasurer to issue certificates of delinquency once three years have passed from the date of delinquency, then foreclose the tax liens in the county's name. The treasurer must give notice to the owner and anyone with a recorded interest, who then has thirty days after service to appear and defend or pay what is due.

Before any sale, the treasurer must run a title search to confirm the legal description and the record titleholder, and that person is treated as the owner for notice purposes. The statute also bars a certificate of delinquency when the total delinquency is $100 or less, not counting interest and penalties, except on parcels a local government has declared a nuisance.

Treasurers must also tell delinquent owners where to get help, including the statewide foreclosure hotline recommended by the Washington State Housing Finance Commission. Roughly two years into a delinquency, the treasurer passes the owner's name and address to a homeownership resource center or other designated entity.

How are taxes and excise tax handled when I sell a Washington house?

The tax lien runs from January 1, so the year's bill follows the property until it is paid. RCW 84.60.020 says that when the sale agreement is silent, the seller is liable for the share of that year's tax that matches the part of the calendar year before the day of sale, and the buyer takes the rest. Most contracts state their own split, and escrow normally settles it at closing. If you owe back taxes, ask the county treasurer for a payoff figure that includes interest through the closing date.

Selling also triggers the real estate excise tax. The Department of Revenue's REET page says the seller usually pays it, it is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, and an unpaid balance can become a lien on the property. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the state portion is 1.1 percent of the price up to $551,000, 1.28 percent from there to $1,551,000, 2.75 percent to $3,051,000, and 3 percent above that. Local excise tax is added on top, and interest runs on unpaid tax after one month. Your closing agent will put the exact figure on the settlement statement.

Sellers who need to move quickly with taxes owed, repairs pending or a tenant in place can ask a cash buyer to price those items into an as-is offer. The settlement statement shows the tax payoff as a line item, so you see exactly what is taken from proceeds.

More questions about Washington Property Tax Guide

What is the deadline to appeal my Washington property value?

It is the latest of July 1, thirty days after the notice was mailed or sent electronically, or a county-adopted window of up to sixty days. The county board of equalization can waive a missed deadline for good cause, such as serious illness, a flood or a documented postal delay (RCW 84.40.038).

Can I pay Washington property tax in two payments?

Yes, when the tax on a parcel is $50 or more. Half is due by April 30 and the rest by October 31. Treasurers may also offer payment agreements or partial payments, so ask your county treasurer what is available.

How much interest do late Washington property taxes carry?

Residential parcels with four or fewer units pay 9 percent a year, computed monthly, with no penalty. Nonresidential property, larger multifamily buildings and personal property pay 12 percent, and the last two groups also face a 3 percent penalty on June 1 and 8 percent more on December 1.

Do I have to pay property tax if I qualify for a senior exemption or deferral?

An exemption reduces what you owe, based on income, home value and levy rates. A deferral postpones payment and adds 5 percent simple interest, which comes due when the home is sold, the owner dies, or the home stops being the primary residence. Your county assessor handles both applications.

Who pays property tax at closing when I sell my house in Washington?

The sale agreement decides. If it says nothing, the seller owes the share of the year's tax matching the days before the sale and the buyer owes the rest (RCW 84.60.020). Escrow usually calculates this on the settlement statement, along with the seller's real estate excise tax.

Washington offers property tax relief for qualifying homeowners, and official sources explain the rules.

What the official sources say

  • Homestead exemption amount (protection from creditors) is the greater of $125,000 or the county median sale price of a single-family home in the preceding calendar year (with no dollar limit in a specified state-income-tax-on-pension judgment case). (RCW 6.13.030; source)

What is the Washington homestead exemption?

The Washington homestead exemption protects the equity in your home from most unsecured creditors. It is set out in chapter 6.13 of the Revised Code of Washington, and the legislature described its purpose in 2021 as protecting a homeowner's equity in a home against unsecured creditors.

The protected amount applies to the net value of the home, which the statute defines as market value less liens and encumbrances that rank ahead of the judgment being collected. A mortgage balance therefore comes off the top before the exemption is measured. If you owe a creditor with a judgment against you, the exemption decides how much of your equity the creditor can reach and how much stays with you.

This is a creditor-protection rule. It is separate from any property tax break for seniors or disabled owners, which the county assessor handles. Anyone selling a Washington house with a judgment, a lien or a bankruptcy in the background should understand both questions before accepting an offer.

How much equity does the exemption protect in Washington?

Under RCW 6.13.030, the exemption is the greater of $125,000 or the county median sale price of a single-family home in the preceding calendar year. For homes in higher-priced counties the second number usually controls, so the protection depends on where the house sits.

The statute tells courts to take the median price from the Washington Center for Real Estate Research, or from a successor entity designated by the Office of Financial Management if that center stops publishing the data. There is also a third rule: where a state is trying to collect income tax on pension or retirement benefits earned while the owner lived in Washington, the homestead has no dollar limit.

  • Floor: $125,000 of net equity.
  • Higher-value counties: the prior year's county median single-family sale price, if it is larger.
  • Pension income tax judgments from another state: no dollar cap.

For the current median in your county, ask the court clerk or the attorney handling the matter which published figure the court is using.

Do I have to file anything to claim a homestead?

Usually no. A home you live in as your principal residence is protected automatically from the moment you occupy it, under RCW 6.13.040. The homestead can be a house, a mobile home (whether or not it is permanently attached to the land), or land you own intending to put a home on and live there.

A written declaration is required only when you select a homestead from land you do not yet occupy. In that case the owner signs a declaration of homestead, acknowledged the same way a deed is, and records it with the recording officer of the county where the land lies. The declaration must state that you live on the premises or intend to, give the legal description, and estimate the actual cash value.

If you already claim another parcel as your homestead, you must also record a declaration of abandonment for that parcel. That second document states that the property is no longer your homestead, includes the legal description, and gives the date of abandonment. Ask the county auditor's recording office for its current format and fee.

What happens to the exemption if I move out or sell?

Washington presumes a homestead abandoned when the owner vacates it for six months in a row. If you will be away longer, you have no other principal residence and you do not mean to give up the home, RCW 6.13.050 lets you record a declaration of nonabandonment with the county. It must say you intend to return, say where you will live in the meantime, estimate how long you will be gone, give the reason, and describe the property.

Selling does not erase the protection right away. Under RCW 6.13.070, proceeds from a voluntary, good-faith sale made to buy a new homestead are exempt for one year from receipt, up to the statutory amount, and so is the new homestead bought with them. Insurance money paid for a destroyed home gets the same one-year treatment when it is held to restore or replace the house.

That one-year window matters if you plan to sell, rent for a while and then buy again. Keep the sale proceeds identifiable, and talk to an attorney before spending them on anything other than a replacement home.

Which debts can reach a Washington homestead?

The exemption does not shield the house from every creditor. RCW 6.13.080 lists the debts that can be enforced against it regardless of the protected amount.

  • Debts secured by mechanic's, laborer's, construction, material supplier's, vendor's, maritime or automobile repair liens on that property.
  • Debts secured by a security agreement covering the property, or by a mortgage or deed of trust signed and acknowledged by both spouses or both domestic partners, or by an unmarried owner.
  • Court-ordered child support and maintenance.
  • Medical assistance the state paid correctly on your behalf.
  • Condominium, homeowners' or common interest community association liens.
  • Sales and related taxes collected but not sent to the Department of Revenue.

In practice this means a first mortgage, a home equity loan you signed, a contractor's lien and unpaid association assessments all stay attached to the property and must be paid or cleared at closing. The exemption mostly matters against unsecured judgment creditors such as credit card or medical collectors.

How does a judgment lien affect selling a home in Washington?

A judgment against a homestead owner becomes a lien on the value above the homestead exemption once the creditor records the judgment with the county recording officer, according to RCW 6.13.090. A Department of Revenue tax warrant becomes such a lien when it is filed in superior court. A seller with a recorded judgment should ask the closing agent how that lien will be paid at closing.

If a creditor tries to force a sale, the process runs through the superior court. The creditor petitions for an appraiser, the owner gets at least ten days' notice of the hearing, and the appraiser reports within fifteen days of appointment. If the net value exceeds the exemption and the land can be divided without material injury, the court can set off the exempt portion to the owner. If it cannot, the court orders a sale at which no bid below the exemption amount may be accepted.

Sale money is then paid out in a fixed order: first the homestead exemption to the owner, then the creditor up to the execution amount, and any balance to the owner. The cash paid to you keeps the same protection as the home.

What do spouses and domestic partners need to sign?

Both spouses or both state-registered domestic partners must sign and acknowledge any deed or mortgage of a homestead, under RCW 6.13.060. A power of attorney for conveying or encumbering the homestead is the allowed exception. A dependent who is not a spouse or partner does not have to sign.

If one spouse or partner is incompetent or disabled and no guardian has been appointed, the other may apply to the superior court in the county of the homestead for an order allowing a sale or mortgage. The statute requires a sworn petition filed thirty days before the hearing and notice by publication once a week for three weeks. Once the order is entered, the sale carries the same effect as if the applicant owned the property outright.

Sellers in this situation should plan on the court timeline before setting a closing date.

Sale proceedsExempt for one year when used for a new homesteadRCW 6.13.070
Judgment lienAttaches to value above the exemption when recordedRCW 6.13.090

More questions about Washington Homestead Exemption

Is the Washington homestead exemption the same as a property tax exemption?

No. The exemption in chapter 6.13 RCW shields home equity from creditors. Property tax relief for seniors, disabled owners and others is a separate program run through the county assessor, so ask the assessor's office about it.

Does a Washington homestead protect my home from foreclosure by my mortgage lender?

No. Under RCW 6.13.080 the exemption is unavailable against debts secured by a mortgage or deed of trust that both spouses or partners (or an unmarried owner) signed, so the lender can still enforce its lien.

Can I keep the money if I sell my homestead?

Yes, within limits. Proceeds from a good-faith voluntary sale made to buy a new homestead stay exempt for one year from receipt, up to the statutory amount, and the replacement home is protected too.

What if I rent the house out or leave for more than six months?

A homestead is presumed abandoned after six continuous months away. If you do not intend to abandon it and have no other principal residence, record a declaration of nonabandonment with the county before the gap grows.

Does the homestead amount change from county to county?

Yes. The floor is $125,000, but where the prior calendar year's county median single-family sale price is higher, that figure applies, using data from the Washington Center for Real Estate Research.

This guide covers what official sources say about Washington estate and inheritance tax.

What the official sources say

  • Washington estate tax exclusion amount: $3,076,000 for decedents dying Jan 1 to before July 1, 2026, and $3,000,000 for decedents dying on or after July 1, 2026. (RCW 83.100.020; source)
  • For decedents dying on or after July 1, 2025 and before July 1, 2026, graduated rates run from 10% on the first $1M up to 35% above $9M (table on page). (RCW 83.100.040; source)
  • For decedents dying on or after July 1, 2026, the page's table shows rates from 10% up to 20% above $9,000,000. (RCW 83.100.040; source)

Does Washington have an estate tax that affects an inherited house?

Yes. Washington taxes the transfer of property at death once an estate passes the exclusion amount, and a house counts toward the total. The Department of Revenue describes it as a tax on the right to transfer property at death. It is figured on the value of the whole estate, not on what each heir receives, and the estate itself is a taxpayer under RCW 83.100.020.

For heirs who plan to sell, the practical question is whether the estate owes tax, whether a return has to be filed, and whether the state's claim on the property has been released before closing. The answers depend on the date of death, so gather that date first.

What is the Washington estate tax exclusion amount?

The exclusion amount depends on when the person died. RCW 83.100.020 lists $2,193,000 for deaths on or after July 1, 2018 and before July 1, 2025. It lists $3,000,000 for deaths from July 1, 2025 up to January 1, 2026, then $3,076,000 for January 1 through June 30, 2026, and $3,000,000 for deaths on or after July 1, 2026.

The statute also contains an annual inflation formula that begins with deaths in 2027. For a death in 2027 or later, ask the Department of Revenue which amount applies to your date.

Nonresidents can be pulled in too. The department says a person who lived elsewhere but owned Washington real estate or tangible personal property may owe, and the tax on such an estate is reduced by a fraction based on how much of the gross estate sits in the state.

What are the Washington estate tax rates?

Rates are graduated and start at 10 percent. For estates of people who died on or after July 1, 2026, RCW 83.100.040 sets the schedule below, applied to the Washington taxable estate. That figure is the gross estate less allowed deductions and the exclusion amount.

Washington taxable estateInitial taxPlus rate on the excess
$0 to $1,000,000$010%
$1,000,000 to $2,000,000$100,00014%
$2,000,000 to $3,000,000$240,00015%
$3,000,000 to $4,000,000$390,00016%
$4,000,000 to $6,000,000$550,00018%
$6,000,000 to $7,000,000$910,00019%
$7,000,000 to $9,000,000$1,100,00019.5%
Above $9,000,000$1,490,00020%

Deaths between July 1, 2025 and July 1, 2026 fall under a steeper schedule in the same section, with a 35 percent top rate above $9,000,000. Deaths before July 1, 2025 use a third table. The department's own worked example, for a 2024 death, takes a $4,000,000 gross estate, subtracts $100,000 of deductions and the $2,193,000 exclusion, and arrives at a taxable estate of $1,707,000 and a tax of $198,980.

Does the estate have to file a return even if no tax is due?

Often, yes. Under RCW 83.100.050 a Washington return is required when the gross estate equals or exceeds the exclusion amount. The Department of Revenue states that a filing is required in that case even if no tax is due. An estate below the threshold files nothing.

There is one carve-out for married couples. A return is not required when the decedent left a surviving spouse, the qualifying family residence passed to that spouse, no election requires a return, and the gross estate less the value of that residence is below the exclusion amount. The statute defines the qualifying family residence as the principal home of the marital community or domestic partnership at the date of death.

  • The filing threshold is the gross estate, which covers assets owned or held in trust wherever they are located.
  • Residents and nonresidents with Washington real property can both be required to file.
  • A return is judged by the date of death, so an estate for a death in early 2026 uses different figures than one from late 2026.

When is Washington estate tax due, and what happens if it is late?

The return and the payment are both due nine months after the date of death. A request for extension, together with an estimated payment, is due on the same day. The Department of Revenue allows a six-month extension to file, but an extension to file is not an extension to pay. Any tax unpaid after nine months accrues interest daily.

Late filing can add a penalty. Under RCW 83.100.070 the penalty is 5 percent of the tax due for each month the return is late, capped at the lesser of 25 percent of the tax or $1,500, and there is no penalty when a return is filed voluntarily before the department sends written notice. The interest rate is reset each January.

Returns and payments can be sent through My DOR or mailed to the Department of Revenue, PO Box 47474, Olympia, WA 98504-7474. The estate tax examiners can be reached at 360-704-5906 or estates@dor.wa.gov.

How does the estate tax connect to selling the house?

The connection is the state's claim against the estate's property. RCW 83.100.080 says the department issues a release once the tax due has been paid, and after the release all property subject to the tax is free of the state's claim for it. If an estate is large enough to owe, ask the department how to obtain that release before you list the house, so the sale is not held up.

Timing also matters for cash, because payment is due nine months after the date of death. If there is tax due and the house is the main asset, speak with the estate's attorney about whether to sell first and pay from the proceeds.

Do heirs pay real estate excise tax when they inherit or sell a Washington house?

Receiving the house by will or inheritance is not subject to real estate excise tax, according to WAC 458-61A-202. That holds whether or not a mortgage is attached to the property. The documentation goes to the county treasurer where the property sits and might include a certified death certificate, letters testamentary or letters of administration for a probated estate, or a signed lack of probate affidavit when no probate happens.

A later sale is a different event. The rule states that a transfer from an heir to a third party is subject to the tax, and its example has an heir selling an inherited house for $50,000 and owing tax on the full $50,000. The same rule says that when one heir pays siblings to take sole title, the tax is due on the amount paid, which is $120,000 in its example.

On the income tax side, the IRS says property received through inheritance has its basis determined under Publication 551 rather than by simple cost. Ask a tax preparer for the figure before you set a price.

More questions about Washington Estate and Inheritance Tax

What is the Washington estate tax exclusion for 2026?

It is $3,076,000 for deaths from January 1 through June 30, 2026, and $3,000,000 for deaths on or after July 1, 2026. These figures come from RCW 83.100.020 and the Department of Revenue.

What is the top Washington estate tax rate?

For deaths on or after July 1, 2026 the top rate is 20 percent on the portion of the taxable estate above $9,000,000. For deaths from July 1, 2025 to July 1, 2026 the top rate is 35 percent above $9,000,000.

When is the Washington estate tax return due?

Nine months after the date of death. A six-month extension to file is available, but the tax itself is still due at nine months, and interest accrues daily on any unpaid amount.

Do I owe real estate excise tax when I inherit a house in Washington?

No. Transfers by will or inheritance are not subject to the tax. A later sale of the house by the heir to a buyer is subject to it, based on the full sale price.

Can an estate file a Washington return when no tax is owed?

An estate must file if its gross estate equals or exceeds the exclusion amount, even when the tax comes to zero. Estates below the exclusion amount do not file, and a limited exception exists for a family residence that passes to a surviving spouse.

Washington charges a tax or fee on real estate transfers, as described below.

What the official sources say

  • State REET rates from Jan 1, 2020: 1.1% of selling price up to $500,000; 1.28% above $500,000 to $1,500,000; 2.75% above $1.5M to $3M; 3% above $3M. (RCW 82.45.060; source)
  • The REET is the obligation of the seller; the Department of Revenue may enforce it by action of debt against the seller or by foreclosure in the manner of mortgages. (RCW 82.45.080; source)
  • Usually the seller pays REET, but if they do not the buyer is responsible. (Real estate excise tax | Washington Department of Revenue; source)
  • REET is due to the county treasurer where the property is located on the date of sale, regardless of when the sale is recorded. (Real estate excise tax | Washington Department of Revenue; source)
  • Agricultural land and timberland remain subject to a flat 1.28% state REET rate. (Real estate excise tax | Washington Department of Revenue; source)
  • An affidavit is required for exempt transfers such as a transfer from a court order, deed in lieu of foreclosure, or a community property agreement; taxpayer must keep supporting documentation at least four years (RCW 82.45.100). (Real estate excise tax | Washington Department of Revenue; source)
Selling in Washington?
We buy Washington houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How much is the Washington real estate excise tax on a home sale?

Washington charges a graduated state excise tax on each sale of real property, starting at 1.1 percent of the selling price and rising to 3 percent on the top slice. The rates come from RCW 82.45.060. Each rate applies only to the part of the price that falls inside its band, so a sale is never taxed at 2.75 percent across the board.

The dollar thresholds are adjusted every fourth year. The Department of Revenue shows the band limits for sales through the end of 2026 and a new set for sales beginning January 1, 2027, so a closing in December 2026 and one in January 2027 use different numbers.

State ratePortion of price, through Dec. 31, 2026Portion of price, from Jan. 1, 2027
1.1%Up to $525,000Up to $551,000
1.28%$525,000.01 to $1,525,000$551,000.01 to $1,551,000
2.75%$1,525,000.01 to $3,025,000$1,551,000.01 to $3,051,000
3.0%Over $3,025,000Over $3,051,000

Source: Washington Department of Revenue, real estate excise tax page.

Land classified as agricultural land or timberland is taxed at a flat 1.28 percent state rate instead. The county assessor assigns that classification, and the buyer must state that the land will keep qualifying use.

Who pays the tax in Washington, and when is it due?

The seller pays. The Department of Revenue says the seller usually pays and that the buyer becomes responsible if the seller does not, and RCW 82.45.080 calls the tax the seller's obligation. The tax is due to the county treasurer in the county where the house sits, on the date of sale, even if the deed is recorded later.

The date of sale is the day the deed is signed and delivered to the buyer or the buyer's agent. The Department of Revenue treats that as the date the deed is notarized unless someone can prove a different date. Timing matters because of these rules in RCW 82.45.100:

  • Tax not paid within one month of the sale starts to carry interest from the date of sale.
  • A penalty of 5 percent applies after one month, 10 percent after two months and 20 percent after three months.
  • The penalties can be collected from the seller only.
  • If the tax is late, the buyer is personally liable unless a document showing the sale is recorded in the county's property records.

The Department of Revenue lists the interest rate for 2026 and for 2027 at 6 percent. In practice an escrow or title company collects the tax from the seller's proceeds at closing, so most sellers never write a separate check.

Is there a local tax on top of the state tax?

Yes. The state tax is only the first layer, and the Department of Revenue states that the local tax must be calculated and added to the graduated state rate for the total due. Under RCW 82.46.010, a county or city may impose a tax of up to 0.25 percent of the selling price, and may impose an additional tax of up to 0.5 percent in lieu of a different local option listed in RCW 82.14.030(2).

The local rate depends on the location code of the property, which can differ between an incorporated city and the unincorporated county around it. Ask the county treasurer or your escrow officer for the exact combined rate before you set a net-proceeds number. Local revenue is meant for capital projects such as streets, parks and water and sewer systems.

Which Washington property transfers are exempt from the excise tax?

Washington allows only a limited list of exemptions, and only one can be claimed per transfer. The exemption code goes in section 7 of the affidavit, and the seller should keep the paperwork that proves it. The rules sit in chapter 458-61A of the Washington Administrative Code. The ones that come up most often for homeowners are below.

  • Inheritance or devise. WAC 458-61A-202 exempts transfers by will or inheritance, whether or not a mortgage is attached. A later sale by the heir is taxable on the full price. An heir who buys out siblings with cash owes tax on that cash.
  • Gifts. Under WAC 458-61A-201, a gift with no consideration is not a sale. If the person receiving the house takes over the mortgage payments, that counts as consideration and the debt is taxed. Both parties sign a supplemental statement.
  • Foreclosure transfers. WAC 458-61A-208 exempts trustee's sales, court-ordered mortgage foreclosure sales, sheriff's sales on a judgment, and deeds in lieu of foreclosure when no extra consideration passes.
  • Condemnation. A sale to a government under written notice of eminent domain is exempt under WAC 458-61A-206.
  • Bankruptcy. Transfers by a trustee after a confirmed chapter 11 or 12 plan are exempt under WAC 458-61A-207.

An ordinary arm's-length sale of a house to a buyer, including a sale of an inherited or distressed house, does not fall into any of these. It is taxed on the full selling price.

What paperwork does a seller file, and where?

A seller files a real estate excise tax affidavit with the county treasurer, together with the deed and the payment. The Department of Revenue says a deeded transfer goes to the treasurer of the county where the property is located, and that mailing the affidavit and deed to the Department by mistake can delay the filing and cause penalties and interest. Forms are on the Department of Revenue site.

Which affidavit you use depends on the property. A single location affidavit covers one or more parcels inside one local jurisdiction code. A multiple locations affidavit with a worksheet is needed when the parcels sit in different jurisdiction codes, even inside one county. The affidavit can be signed by an agent for the seller or buyer, and electronic signatures count when proper authentication is used.

Keep records that support the price and any exemption for at least four years. All sales are subject to audit, and under RCW 82.45.100 the Department generally cannot assess or refund more than four years after the sale unless there was fraud, a misstatement of a material fact or a failure to report the sale. A refund request is also due within four years and goes through the county treasurer for a deeded transfer.

What happens if the tax is never paid?

Unpaid tax can become a lien on the property, and the state has two ways to collect from the seller. Under RCW 82.45.080 the Department of Revenue may bring an action of debt against the seller, or may proceed the way a lender would in a mortgage foreclosure, and using one route does not rule out the other. The Department also audits transactions after the fact and will assess additional tax with interest and penalties if a price was understated or an exemption was claimed without support.

Controlling interest transfers have their own rule. When 50 percent or more of an entity that owns Washington real estate changes hands within 36 months, the Department of Revenue treats it as a sale of the real property, and the return is due within five days of the transfer. Anyone selling a house held in an LLC or partnership should ask the Department of Revenue REET team before moving ownership interests.

More questions about Washington Real Estate Transfer Tax

Does the buyer or the seller pay the Washington real estate excise tax?

The seller pays. State law makes the tax the seller's obligation, and the buyer becomes responsible only if the seller fails to pay. In most closings the escrow company deducts the tax from the seller's proceeds and sends it to the county treasurer.

How much state excise tax is owed on a $600,000 house sold in 2026?

The state portion is $6,735. That is 1.1 percent of the first $525,000 ($5,775) plus 1.28 percent of the remaining $75,000 ($960). The local tax for the city or county is added on top, so ask the treasurer or escrow officer for the final figure.

Do I owe the tax if I give my house to a family member?

Not if the transfer is a true gift with no payment or debt assumption. A gift needs a supplemental statement signed by both parties. If the person receiving the house starts paying your mortgage, the Department of Revenue treats the debt as consideration and taxes it.

How long do I have to pay before penalties start?

You have one month from the date of sale. After that, interest runs from the sale date, and penalties of 5, 10 and 20 percent apply at one, two and three months. The penalties are collected from the seller only.

Is an inherited house taxed when it passes to the heirs?

No. A transfer by will or inheritance is exempt, even with a mortgage on the property. The exemption ends when the heir sells to a third party, because that sale is taxed on the full price. Estate documents such as letters testamentary or a death certificate support the claim.

This guide covers what official sources say about Washington tax on a house sale.

What the official sources say

  • Washington capital gains excise tax applies only to individuals: 7% of Washington capital gains, plus an additional 2.90% on the portion exceeding $1,000,000 beginning Jan 1, 2025. (RCW 82.87.040; source)
  • The chapter does not apply to sale or exchange of real estate transferred by deed, real estate contract, judgment or other instrument that transfers title to real property recorded with the counties. (RCW 82.87.050; source)
Selling in Washington?
We buy Washington houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Washington's capital gains tax apply when I sell my house?

No. Washington's capital gains excise tax does not apply to the sale of real estate that transfers by a deed or similar instrument recorded with the county. That exemption is written into RCW 82.87.050, and the Department of Revenue lists real estate first among the assets the tax leaves alone.

The tax itself is set out in RCW 82.87.040. It is a 7 percent excise on an individual's Washington capital gains, with an added 2.90 percent on the part of those gains above $1,000,000 starting January 1, 2025. Only individuals pay it. A seller of a Washington house who also sold stock or a business interest in the same year may still owe it on those other sales, but the house closing itself stays outside the chapter.

What kinds of real estate sales fall under the exemption?

The exemption reaches a sale or exchange of real estate transferred by deed, real estate contract, judgment, or another instrument that moves title and is filed as a public record in the county where the land sits. An ordinary Washington house sale transfers title by deed, so it fits. A contract sale where you carry the financing for the buyer also fits, since a real estate contract is named in the statute.

The same section reaches into entities in a narrower way. If you own an interest in a privately held company and sell that interest, the exemption covers only the part of your gain that comes from real estate the company owns directly. Real estate the company does not own directly is left out of that calculation.

  • Property that is depreciable under federal tax law is exempt under its own subsection.
  • Assets inside a 401(k), 403(b), IRA or similar retirement account are exempt.
  • Timber and timberland are exempt, as are some livestock and commercial fishing privileges.

What are the Washington capital gains rates and deductions for other assets?

The state subtracts a standard deduction before it applies the rate. RCW 82.87.060 sets it at $250,000 per individual, or $250,000 combined for spouses and domestic partners, and the amount is adjusted for inflation. The Department of Revenue reports $270,000 for 2024 and $278,000 for 2025.

Other deductions cover gain from selling a qualified family-owned small business and certain charitable gifts. A credit is available when another state or country taxed the same gain, limited to the smaller of the Washington tax on those assets or the tax paid elsewhere. Losses do not carry forward into later years under the Washington tax.

What tax do I pay when I sell a house in Washington, then?

The state tax that applies to a Washington house sale is the real estate excise tax, usually called REET. The Department of Revenue says all sales of real property in the state are subject to it unless a specific exemption applies. The seller usually pays. If the seller does not, the buyer becomes responsible, and an unpaid tax can become a lien on the property.

REET is due to the county treasurer where the property sits on the date of sale, whatever date the deed gets recorded. The date of sale is the date the deed is notarized. Penalty and interest start if the tax is unpaid one month after that date. The affidavit, the deed and the payment go to the county treasurer.

The state portion is graduated. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue lists these tiers, with the local REET added on top:

  • 1.1 percent on the part of the price up to $551,000.
  • 1.28 percent on the part from $551,000 to $1,551,000.
  • 2.75 percent on the part from $1,551,000 to $3,051,000.
  • 3.0 percent on the part above $3,051,000.

Agricultural land and timberland stay at a flat 1.28 percent state rate. For a closing before January 1, 2027, ask the county treasurer which thresholds apply and what the local rate is in your city.

Will I owe federal tax on the gain from my Washington house?

Possibly, though many sellers owe nothing. The IRS lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain on the sale of your main home, or up to $500,000 on a joint return. To qualify you must meet an ownership test and a use test, which means owning and living in the home for at least 24 months of the 5 years before the sale. The two periods do not have to match, and generally you cannot use the exclusion if you excluded gain from another home sale in the prior two years.

Reporting is a separate matter. If you receive a Form 1099-S you must report the sale even when the whole gain is excludable, and you must also report it when you cannot exclude all of the gain. The sale goes on Form 8949 and Schedule D when required. IRS Publication 523 holds the worksheets.

Your gain is the sale price less your adjusted basis. Basis starts with what you paid and rises with improvements that add value. For a house you received by gift or inheritance, the IRS points to Publication 551 for how basis is set, so an inherited Washington house can have a very different basis than one you bought.

When are Washington capital gains returns and payments due?

If you do owe the state tax on other assets, the return is due the same day as your federal income tax return. Everyone files electronically through My DOR, attaching a copy of the federal return. An extension is available only if you already have a federal extension and you request the state one through My DOR on or before April 15. An extension does not move the payment date.

Payment is typically due April 15, unless that falls on a weekend or holiday. Beginning with tax year 2026 you may prepay up to six months before the due date. Late returns and late payments carry penalties and interest. Paying less than 80 percent of the tax due counts as a substantial underpayment and adds its own penalty. If you request an extension or make a payment, a return must be filed even when no tax turns out to be due.

How should a Washington seller plan around these taxes?

Start with the closing date. REET is calculated on the full selling price, so know the price tier before you accept an offer, and ask the county treasurer or your closing agent for the combined state and local figure. Keep the documents that support the price and any exemption you claim for at least four years, since all transactions are subject to audit by the Department of Revenue.

Next, separate the house from everything else you sold that year. A house sold by deed sits outside the capital gains excise tax. Stock, a business interest or other investments may not. Your tax preparer can total those and apply the standard deduction. Last, run the federal numbers: ownership dates, residence dates, improvements and any depreciation you claimed if part of the home was a rental.

If the house is inherited, behind on payments, or has repairs you cannot afford, the same taxes apply to the sale. Call the Department of Revenue, the county treasurer, or a tax professional before you sign anything with a price attached.

More questions about Washington Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Is there a Washington capital gains tax on selling a primary residence?

No. Real estate transferred by a recorded deed is exempt under RCW 82.87.050, so a house sale does not trigger the state capital gains excise tax. The real estate excise tax (REET) still applies to the sale, and federal rules on gain apply separately.

Who pays the real estate excise tax in Washington?

The seller usually pays it. If the seller does not, the buyer becomes responsible, and unpaid tax can create a lien on the property. It is paid to the county treasurer where the property is located and is due on the date of sale.

How much of my home sale gain can I exclude on my federal return?

Up to $250,000, or up to $500,000 on a joint return, if you meet the ownership and use tests. You need to have owned and lived in the home for at least 24 months of the 5 years before the sale.

What is the Washington capital gains tax rate?

The rate is 7 percent of an individual's Washington capital gains, plus 2.90 percent on the portion above $1,000,000 beginning January 1, 2025. A standard deduction applies first, and the Department of Revenue reports $278,000 for 2025.

When is the real estate excise tax due on a Washington house sale?

It is due on the date of sale, which is the date the deed is notarized, and it goes to the county treasurer. Penalty and interest begin if it is not paid within one month of that date.

Washington evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law.

What the official sources say

  • For nonpayment of rent, a tenant under chapter 59.18 who does not comply within 14 days after service of a pay-or-vacate notice is guilty of unlawful detainer. (RCW 59.12.030; source)
  • A landlord ending a periodic tenancy serves notice more than 20 days before the end of the period (as stated in this section). (RCW 59.12.030; source)
  • Three days' notice to quit applies to waste, unlawful business or nuisance. (RCW 59.12.030; source)
  • A tenant who continues in possession after the owner elects to sell a single-family residence may be evicted if the landlord gave at least 90 days' advance written notice. Page shown is labeled effective Jan 1, 2028. (RCW 59.18.650; source)
  • The owner 'elects to sell' by making reasonable attempts within 30 days after the tenant vacates, including listing at a reasonable price with a realty agency or on the MLS. Page shown is labeled effective Jan 1, 2028. (RCW 59.18.650; source)
  • Landlord must give at least 120 days' written notice to end tenancies for demolition, substantial rehabilitation or change of use, and 120 days for condominium conversion. Page shown is labeled effective Jan 1, 2028. (RCW 59.18.200; source)
Selling in Washington?
We buy Washington houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What are the steps in a Washington eviction?

A Washington eviction is a court case called unlawful detainer, and it moves in five stages: a written notice, a summons and complaint filed in superior court, a hearing, a judgment, and a writ of restitution that returns possession to the landlord. A landlord cannot skip to the last step. Removing a tenant in violation of RCW 59.18.650 exposes the owner to a wrongful eviction claim.

The process matters to anyone selling a rented house because each stage adds time and each has rules the tenant can use. Owners who plan to sell should map the dates before they list.

StageWhat happensSource
NoticeWritten notice served, 14 days for unpaid rent or 10 days for other lease breachesRCW 59.12.030
Summons and complaintTenant gets a deadline to respond in writingRCW 59.18.365
HearingCourt hears answers and defenses and may order a writRCW 59.18.380
JudgmentRestitution of the premises, rent and damages, costsRCW 59.18.410
Writ of restitutionClerk of the superior court issues it, with a bond if before judgmentRCW 59.12.090

How does a landlord start the eviction case?

After the notice period ends with no payment or fix, the landlord files in superior court and has a summons served on the tenant. RCW 59.18.365 gives the form. It sets a response deadline of 5:00 p.m. on a stated date and warns that phone calls to the landlord or the landlord's lawyer are not a response.

A tenant can respond with a notice of appearance. That is a letter stating the tenant is appearing in the case, naming the landlords and tenants, and giving the tenant's name, mailing address for legal papers, signature, phone number if any, and the case number if filed. A response sent by mail must go out three days before the deadline, and a hand-delivered or faxed one by the deadline itself.

The tenant who responds is notified of a hearing date in an order to show cause. A tenant who ignores that notice and does not attend can be evicted, and the landlord might also charge more money. The summons tells a tenant who moves out before the court date to inform the landlord.

What happens at the Washington show cause hearing?

At the hearing on the landlord's motion for a writ, the tenant or anyone in possession may answer, orally or in writing, and raise any legal or equitable defense or set-off arising out of the tenancy. The court examines the parties and witnesses to decide whether the landlord has the right to possession. The rules sit in RCW 59.18.380.

If the landlord shows a right to possession, the court orders a writ of restitution returnable ten days after its date and sets the rest of the case for trial in the usual way. If the landlord does not, the court denies the writ and sends the case to trial within thirty days. In a nonpayment case, a tenant has three days after service of a writ issued before final judgment to stay it by paying all rent found due and then paying the monthly rent while the case continues.

Before a writ issues ahead of final judgment, the landlord must file a bond in an amount the court orders. The bond covers costs and damages the tenant may suffer if the writ was wrongly obtained. Under RCW 59.12.090 the writ is issued by the superior court clerk and is returnable in twenty days.

What does the judgment include and can a tenant get the home back?

If the landlord wins at trial, RCW 59.18.410 directs a judgment restoring the premises and, for rent or lease defaults, declaring the tenancy forfeited. The court also awards the damages tied to the tenancy and any rent found due. Late fees count only if the lease provides them, and the statute caps them at $75 in total. The court may award statutory costs and reasonable attorneys' fees as provided in RCW 59.18.290.

When the case is for unpaid rent, execution waits five court days after judgment. During that window, and before judgment, the tenant or another interested party may pay the rent due, court costs, allowed late fees and any awarded attorneys' fees, and the tenant is restored to the tenancy. A tenant who has a pledge letter of financial assistance from a government or nonprofit agency gets until the date of eviction. A tenant who has already been reinstated after judgment during the past 12 months pays an extra $50 for each time.

Can a court delay the writ after a nonpayment judgment?

Yes, within limits. A court can stay the writ for good cause on fair terms, but the stay cannot run longer than 90 days from the order. The judge weighs listed factors, and the tenant carries the burden of proof.

  • Whether the default was willful or came from circumstances beyond the tenant's control that are unlikely to recur.
  • The tenant's ability to pay the judgment on time and the tenant's payment history.
  • Whether the tenant is otherwise in substantial compliance with the lease.
  • The hardship an eviction would cause, and conduct tied to other notices in the past six months.

A stay brings a payment plan, and the first payment is one month's rent within five court days of the order. If the tenant misses a later payment, the landlord can serve a notice of default and the tenant then has three calendar days to vacate before the sheriff may execute the writ. A tenant who received three or more pay or vacate notices in the prior twelve months cannot seek this relief unless a notice was invalid. The court may also make a finding on whether the landlord can apply to the state landlord mitigation program.

How does the eviction process affect selling a rented Washington house?

It sets the clock. If the sale is the reason you want the tenant out, RCW 59.18.650 requires at least 90 days' written notice for a single-family residence, and the owner is expected to make reasonable attempts to sell, including listing the home, within 30 days after the tenant leaves. A fixed-term lease cannot be cut short on that ground without the tenant's written consent and at least 60 days to vacate.

The tenant also has support. The Attorney General's landlord-tenant page says the court must appoint an attorney for indigent tenants in eviction cases, subject to available funding. The statutory summons and pay or vacate notice point tenants to the Eviction Defense Screening Line, the Northwest Justice Project CLEAR hotline and free or low-cost mediation through dispute resolution centers. Mediation can happen before any court case starts.

If you would rather not run the process yourself, talk with a Washington landlord-tenant attorney or the superior court clerk in your county about filing steps and fees, and ask the county treasurer about taxes due at closing.

More questions about Washington Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a Washington eviction take?

The length depends on the case. The notice runs 14 days for unpaid rent or 10 days for other lease breaches, the tenant then gets a response deadline on the summons, and the court sets a hearing. A stay of up to 90 days can add time after a nonpayment judgment.

Can a Washington landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?

No. Removing a tenant in violation of RCW 59.18.650 makes the landlord liable for wrongful eviction, with damages of the greater of actual loss or three times the monthly rent, plus fees. The landlord has to use the court process and the writ of restitution.

Who carries out a writ of restitution in Washington?

The superior court clerk issues the writ, and the sheriff executes it. RCW 59.18.410 refers to the sheriff serving and executing the writ and not executing it until the required court days or calendar days pass.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying the rent?

In a nonpayment case, often yes. Before judgment or within five court days after it, the tenant may pay the rent due, costs, allowed late fees and awarded attorneys' fees and be restored to the tenancy. A pledge of rental assistance extends the time.

Does a tenant have a right to a lawyer in a Washington eviction?

An indigent tenant is entitled to a court-appointed attorney, subject to available funding, according to the Attorney General. Income at or below 200 percent of the federal poverty level, or receipt of listed public benefits, qualifies a tenant as indigent.

A Washington deed is recorded with the county office named in the sources below.

What the official sources say

  • A quitclaim deed in the statutory form conveys all of the grantor's then-existing legal and equitable rights in the premises, but does not extend to after-acquired title unless words are added expressing that intention. (RCW 64.04.050; source)
  • The county auditor/recording officer records deeds, grants and transfers of real property, mortgages, and releases of mortgages. (RCW 65.04.030; source)
  • Recording fee: $5 for the first page (8.5 x 14 or less) and $1 for each additional page. (RCW 36.18.010; source)

What does a quitclaim deed do in Washington?

A Washington quitclaim deed passes whatever rights the grantor holds in the property on the day it is signed, and nothing more. RCW 64.04.050 says a deed in the statutory quitclaim form, when properly executed, is a good conveyance, release and quitclaim to the grantee and the grantee's heirs and assigns of all the then existing legal and equitable rights of the grantor in the premises described.

The same section adds a limit that matters in practice: the deed does not reach after-acquired title unless words are added saying that is intended. If the grantor later gains a better claim to the land, the deed does not pick it up on its own.

The statutory form is short. It names the grantor and place of residence, states the consideration, says the grantor "conveys and quitclaims" to the grantee all interest in the described real estate, names the county and Washington as the state, and carries a date. The form does not contain the promises about title that a warranty deed makes, so the buyer relies on the grantor's real interest rather than on any assurance in the paper.

What makes a quitclaim deed valid?

Under RCW 64.04.020, every Washington deed must be in writing, signed by the person bound by it, and acknowledged before someone authorized to take acknowledgments. Plan the notary visit before anyone leaves town, because every grantor must be there to sign.

These are the working steps for most family and cleanup transfers:

  • Get the exact legal description from the last recorded deed or from the county auditor.
  • Find the assessor's parcel number, which must appear on the first page.
  • Have every grantor sign in front of a notary.
  • Complete the real estate excise tax affidavit, covered below.
  • Take the deed and affidavit to the county where the land sits and record it.

If the grantor is married or in a registered domestic partnership, ask a Washington attorney whether the spouse or partner must sign.

How do you record a quitclaim deed in Washington?

You record it with the county auditor in the county where the property is located. RCW 65.04.030 lists deeds, grants and transfers of real property among the instruments the auditor or recording officer must record once the fees are paid. The first-page layout is fixed by RCW 65.04.045, so build the first page carefully.

First-page requirementWhat RCW 65.04.045 says
Top marginAt least three inches, with one inch on the bottom and sides
Return addressName and address for return, top left
Document titleImmediately below the three-inch margin
PartiesNames of grantors and grantees
Legal descriptionAbbreviated: lot, block, plat, or section, township, range and quarter section
Parcel numberAssessor's tax parcel or account number, set apart from other text

Source: RCW 65.04.045 (app.leg.wa.gov).

Pages must be no larger than 14 inches long and 8.5 inches wide, with text in eight point type or larger and ink that images clearly. No attachments are allowed except firmly attached bar code or address labels. Except for documents from governmental agencies, the deed may not contain a Social Security number, a date of birth tied to a person, or a parent's maiden name tied to a person.

What does recording a quitclaim deed cost in Washington?

The base recording fee is $5 for the first page and $1 for each added page of 8.5 by 14 inches or less, set by RCW 36.18.010. That statute also adds surcharges on every recorded instrument: $3 for the state library operations account, $2 for the library-archives building account while its financing contract is unpaid, a modernization surcharge, and further assessments set in other sections.

Because those add-ons change, the number on your receipt will be higher than $5. Ask the county auditor's recording office for the full fee for a deed of your page count before you go. Ask the same office how it accepts deeds, whether by mail, at the counter or electronically.

The auditor's fee is separate from the real estate excise tax, which is paid to the county treasurer, so plan for two payments when you submit the deed.

Does a quitclaim deed trigger real estate excise tax in Washington?

Often it does, unless a specific exemption applies. The Department of Revenue's real estate excise tax page says an affidavit is generally required whenever title passes by deed, grant, assignment or quitclaim. The tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, whether or not the deed has been recorded yet. The date of sale is the date the deed is executed and delivered, which the Department treats as the date it is notarized.

A true gift is the most common exemption. Under WAC 458-61A-201, a gift of real property is not a sale because nothing is given in return. Several traps follow from that rule:

  • If the new owner agrees to take over the mortgage, the debt is consideration and tax is due on it, though equity can still be gifted.
  • If the new owner starts making payments on the debt after the transfer, tax can be due on the debt being paid.
  • A refinance involving the new owner within six months of the transfer is presumed to make the transfer a sale. After six months, the presumption runs toward a gift.
  • Both grantor and grantee must sign a supplemental statement that goes with the affidavit, and the grantor must keep records in case of audit.

Other exemptions cover moving a home into a revocable trust and taking it back out without payment, and a deed between the same owners that only changes how they hold title, such as tenants in common becoming joint tenants (WAC 458-61A-211). Only one exemption may be claimed per transfer.

When is a quitclaim deed the wrong tool for selling a house?

It is the wrong tool whenever the buyer needs reliable title. Because the deed hands over only what the grantor has, a buyer who pays real money for a quitclaim gets no statement in the paper that the title is good. For a sale, ask a Washington title company or attorney what the closing will need.

A quitclaim fits better for moves among people who already trust each other, such as adding or removing a spouse after a divorce, placing a home in a revocable trust, or clearing a possible claim from an old record. If the house is in probate, the nonintervention powers in RCW 11.68.090 or a transfer on death deed may be the cleaner path, and the sibling guide on Washington transfer on death deeds covers that route.

If you need to sell a home with title questions, back taxes or heirs who disagree, a cash buyer can review the situation as is. Bring the last recorded deed and any court papers so the closing agent can see what needs to be cleared.

More questions about Washington Quitclaim Deed

Does a quitclaim deed guarantee clear title in Washington?

No. It passes only the grantor's then existing legal and equitable rights in the property, and it does not reach after-acquired title unless the deed says so (RCW 64.04.050). A buyer who wants assurance about title usually asks for more than a quitclaim.

Who records a Washington quitclaim deed?

The county auditor in the county where the property is located records it. The deed must be signed and acknowledged, and the first page must carry the return address, title, parties, abbreviated legal description and the assessor's parcel number.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Washington?

The statutory base is $5 for the first page and $1 for each additional page, plus several surcharges on every recorded instrument. Ask the county auditor for the total for your page count, and plan for a separate real estate excise tax payment to the county treasurer.

Is a quitclaim deed between family members tax free in Washington?

It can be, if it is a true gift with no consideration. Assuming the mortgage, paying on the debt after the transfer, or refinancing with the new owner within six months can make it a taxable sale. A signed supplemental statement from both parties goes with the excise tax affidavit.

Can I use a quitclaim deed to leave my house to someone at my death?

Not as a death transfer. A quitclaim conveys the grantor's existing rights under RCW 64.04.050. Washington's transfer on death deed under chapter 64.80 RCW is the recordable deed that takes effect at the owner's death, and it must be recorded with the county auditor before the owner dies.

Washington Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Washington rules with an attorney.

What is a transfer on death deed in Washington?

It is a recorded deed that names who receives your real estate when you die while leaving you full control of the property until then. Chapter 64.80 RCW, the Washington uniform real property transfer on death act, authorizes it: under RCW 64.80.020 an individual may transfer property to one or more beneficiaries effective at the transferor's death by a transfer on death deed.

The statute calls the deed nontestamentary (RCW 64.80.040), so it is not a will, yet it carries the same capacity standard. The person who makes or revokes one needs the capacity required to make a will (RCW 64.80.050). The act applies to deeds made before, on or after June 12, 2014, for owners who die on or after that date (RCW 64.80.901), and it does not displace other lawful ways of passing property (RCW 64.80.902).

What must a Washington transfer on death deed contain?

It must look like an ordinary recordable deed, say that the transfer happens at your death, and be recorded before you die. RCW 64.80.060 sets three requirements:

  • It contains the essential elements and formalities of a properly recordable deed made during life.
  • It states that the transfer to the designated beneficiary is to occur at the transferor's death.
  • It is recorded before the transferor's death with the auditor of the county where the property is located.

A deed signed but never recorded does not meet the third requirement. Recording also brings in the first-page rules for any recorded instrument: a three-inch top margin, a return address, the document title, grantor and grantee names, an abbreviated legal description and the assessor's parcel number (RCW 65.04.045). The beneficiary does not need to be told, does not need to accept, and does not need to give anything in return (RCW 64.80.070).

The act also bars one use. A transfer on death deed may not serve as a deed in lieu of foreclosure of a deed of trust (RCW 64.80.020).

What can the owner still do while alive?

Almost everything. During your life the deed does not affect your rights or those of any other owner, including the right to sell or borrow against the property (RCW 64.80.090). It also does not create any legal or equitable interest for the beneficiary, and it does not expose the property to the beneficiary's creditors. Your creditors, present and future, keep the same rights they had, even if they know about the deed.

The deed does not affect your eligibility, or the beneficiary's, for any form of public assistance while you are alive. Selling the house while you are alive simply ends the deed's effect, since the transfer applies only to property you own at death (RCW 64.80.100).

The deed is revocable even if it says otherwise (RCW 64.80.030). To revoke, RCW 64.80.080 requires a new instrument that does one of these things:

  • A later transfer on death deed that revokes the earlier one expressly or by inconsistency.
  • A separate instrument of revocation that expressly revokes it.
  • An inter vivos deed that expressly revokes it.

Whichever form you use, you must acknowledge it after the acknowledgment of the deed being revoked, and record it before your death in the county where the first deed is recorded. Marking up or tearing the recorded deed does nothing. If several owners signed, revocation by one does not touch the others' interests, and a deed of community property by both spouses or domestic partners is revoked only by both, unless only one is still living.

What happens to the house at the owner's death?

Title moves to the beneficiary named in the deed, but only if that person outlives you. Under RCW 64.80.100 the interest of a beneficiary who fails to survive lapses. With several beneficiaries, shares pass in equal and undivided parts with no right of survivorship, and a lapsed share goes to the others in proportion to what each holds.

Situation at deathWhat RCW 64.80.100 provides
Beneficiary outlives ownerInterest passes under the deed
Beneficiary dies firstThat beneficiary's interest lapses
Owner was a joint owner with survivorsProperty goes to the surviving joint owners by survivorship
Owner was the last surviving joint ownerThe deed takes effect
Community property, spouse did not join the deedOwner's interest passes under the deed
Community property, spouse joined and survivesThe deed is not effective at that death

Source: RCW 64.80.100 (app.leg.wa.gov).

The beneficiary takes the property subject to every mortgage, lien and contract already on it at the owner's death. That includes liens recorded within twenty-four months after death under RCW 41.05A.090 and 43.20B.080. The transfer comes without covenant or warranty of title, even if the deed says otherwise. A beneficiary is also liable for allowed claims against the probate estate and statutory allowances to a surviving spouse and children, to the extent chapter 64.80 and the cross-referenced estate statutes provide (RCW 64.80.120), and may disclaim all or part of the interest under chapter 11.86 RCW.

Is real estate excise tax due when a transfer on death deed takes effect?

Generally no. The Department of Revenue rule on inheritance, WAC 458-61A-202, exempts a transfer made under a previously recorded transfer on death deed when the owner dies. The paperwork is a certified copy of the death certificate, provided to the county treasurer where the property sits and recorded with the county auditor. There is one exception: if the transfer satisfies a contractual obligation the owner owed to the beneficiary, the tax is due.

The exemption stops at the beneficiary. A later sale by an heir to someone else is a taxable sale, according to the same rule. The Department's real estate excise tax page says the seller usually pays, the tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, and exemptions are claimed by listing a code on the affidavit.

How does a transfer on death deed compare with other routes for a Washington house?

Because a transfer on death deed is nontestamentary, it is one of several tools, and the act itself says it does not limit other methods of passing property (RCW 64.80.902). A will that goes through probate involves a court-appointed personal representative, and the rule on nonpro rata distributions notes that a representative with nonintervention powers may distribute under RCW 11.68.090 without excise tax when no consideration is paid.

The small estate affidavit under RCW 11.62.010 is a different tool. It lets a successor collect debts and personal property that are subject to probate, when the probate estate does not exceed $100,000 less liens and encumbrances, excluding a surviving spouse's community interest, and forty days have passed since the death. That statute speaks of debts and personal property, so check with a Washington attorney before assuming it moves a house.

If you have inherited a house under a transfer on death deed and want to sell without repairs, listing or cleanout, a cash buyer can work from the recorded deed and death certificate. Ask the county auditor and a title company what needs to be recorded first.

More questions about Washington Transfer on Death Deed

Do I have to record a Washington transfer on death deed before I die?

Yes. RCW 64.80.060 requires recording with the auditor of the county where the property is located before the transferor's death. A deed signed but not recorded in time does not meet the statute.

Can I change my mind after recording a transfer on death deed?

Yes. The deed is revocable even if it says it is not. You revoke it with a later transfer on death deed, an instrument of revocation or a deed that expressly revokes it, acknowledged and recorded in the same county before you die.

Does the beneficiary have to be told about the deed?

No. The deed is effective without notice to, delivery to or acceptance by the designated beneficiary during your life, and without any payment or other consideration (RCW 64.80.070).

What if my beneficiary dies before I do?

That beneficiary's interest lapses. If you named several beneficiaries, the lapsed share goes to the others in proportion to their interests in the remaining property (RCW 64.80.100).

Does the beneficiary owe excise tax when the house passes at death?

Generally not. WAC 458-61A-202 exempts a transfer under a recorded transfer on death deed and asks for a certified death certificate. Tax is due if the transfer satisfies a contractual obligation the owner had to the beneficiary.
