How does probate work when a Washington homeowner dies?

Probate in Washington starts when someone delivers the will to the superior court or a personal representative is appointed, and it ends when debts are handled and property is distributed or sold. The personal representative is the person the court puts in charge of the estate, usually the executor named in the will.

Title 11 of the Revised Code of Washington governs the process. Most of the steps that affect a house sale involve three questions: who has authority to sign a deed, which creditors have to be dealt with first, and whether any tax is due on the transfer. This page walks through each one using the statutes and rules in force today.

If you inherited a house and want to sell it, start by finding out who holds authority to sign the deed. The superior court clerk in the county where the decedent lived can tell you which filings the court wants to see.

What must happen first after the death?

Whoever holds the original will has a short deadline. Under RCW 11.20.010, a person with custody of a will must deliver it to the court or to the named executor within thirty days of learning of the death. An executor who holds the will must deliver it to the court within forty days. A person who willfully breaks this rule can be liable for damages to anyone harmed.

After the court appoints a personal representative, the clock starts on notices. The representative has 20 days to serve or mail written notice of the appointment and the probate to each heir, legatee and devisee, and to each beneficiary of a nonprobate asset, whose names and addresses are reasonably known, according to RCW 11.28.237. Proof of that service is filed with the court.

The same section requires notice to the state Department of Social and Health Services office of financial recovery within 30 days of appointment, unless the representative gives creditor notice under chapter 11.40 RCW in that time.

Can an estate skip probate with a small estate affidavit?

Sometimes. The affidavit procedure in RCW 11.62.010 lets a successor collect the decedent's personal property and debts owed to the decedent without opening a probate. It applies only when the probate estate, less liens and encumbrances and not counting a surviving spouse's or partner's community property interest, does not exceed $100,000.

The person signing must state, among other things, that:

  • at least forty days have passed since the death;
  • the decedent lived in Washington;
  • no petition to appoint a personal representative is pending or granted anywhere;
  • all debts, including funeral and burial costs, are paid or provided for;
  • every other successor was notified in writing at least ten days earlier.

A copy of the affidavit with the decedent's Social Security number must be mailed to the DSHS office of financial recovery. The section deals with personal property and debts. If the estate includes a house, ask the superior court clerk or an estate attorney which procedure applies to real property before you line up a buyer.

Who can sell the house, and does the court have to approve?

A personal representative with nonintervention powers can sell without going back to court. RCW 11.68.090 gives that representative the power to mortgage, encumber, lease, sell, exchange, convey and assign the decedent's real and personal property, and to do so without a court order and without notice to or approval from any court.

That freedom comes with duties. The representative must act for the benefit of everyone interested in the estate and use discretionary powers in good faith, with honest judgment and in line with the probated will and the beneficiaries' interests. A will can add to or limit nonintervention powers within the limits the statute sets.

A representative without nonintervention powers does not get that exemption from court procedures, so ask the clerk or an estate attorney which steps apply. For the excise tax paperwork on a probated estate, the Department of Revenue rule calls for a certified copy of the letters showing who the court appointed, so request those from the clerk early.

How are the decedent's creditors handled before a sale closes?

Notice to creditors is optional but protective. Under RCW 11.40.020, a representative who gives notice must file it with the court, publish it once a week for three successive weeks in a legal newspaper in the county where the estate is administered, and mail a copy with the decedent's Social Security number to DSHS. Creditors who become known can be served by mail at any point.

RCW 11.40.051 sets the deadlines for claims. The time a creditor has depends on the notice given:

  • Actual notice received: the later of 30 days after mailing or four months after first publication.
  • No actual notice, creditor not reasonably ascertainable: four months after first publication.
  • No actual notice, creditor reasonably ascertainable: 24 months after the date of death.
  • No notice given at all: 24 months after the date of death.

The bar covers both probate and nonprobate assets.

For a seller, this means distributing sale proceeds too early can leave the representative exposed to claims that surface later.

Is there a tax on transferring an inherited Washington house?

Passing a house to an heir does not trigger the real estate excise tax. Under WAC 458-61A-202, transfers by devise or inheritance are exempt whether or not a mortgage is attached, and a nonpro rata distribution by a personal representative is exempt when authorized by RCW 11.68.090 and no consideration is paid to the representative.

The exemption stops at the heir. If the heir then sells to a third party, the sale is taxable on the full price. The rule's examples show this plainly: a person who inherits a property and sells it for $50,000 owes tax on $50,000, and one who sells on a real estate contract for $100,000 owes tax on $100,000. Buying out a sibling's share with cash is taxable on the amount paid.

Documentation goes to the county treasurer and is recorded with the county auditor. For a probated will, the rule calls for a certified copy of the letters testamentary or letters of administration.

Can an heir contest the will before a sale?

Yes, within four months. RCW 11.24.010 lets any interested person file a petition contesting the validity of a will within four months after it is admitted to probate or rejected. A contest is commenced by filing, but the petitioner must personally serve the personal representative within ninety days or the action is treated as never started. If nobody files and serves in time, the probate or rejection is binding and final.

A house sold soon after a will is admitted can still be affected by a contest filed inside that window. Ask the estate's attorney whether the four months have run before you set a closing date.

More questions about Washington Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do I need probate to sell an inherited house in Washington?

Usually the seller needs authority to sign, which comes from a court-appointed personal representative. The small estate affidavit in RCW 11.62.010 covers personal property and debts, so ask the superior court clerk how real property in a small estate is handled.

Can a personal representative sell without a court hearing?

Yes, if the court granted nonintervention powers. RCW 11.68.090 allows a sale of real property without a court order or notice, though the representative must still act in good faith for the beneficiaries.

How long do creditors have to file claims against an estate?

It depends on notice. A creditor who received actual notice has the later of 30 days or four months after first publication, and a known creditor who received none has 24 months from the date of death under RCW 11.40.051.

Is real estate excise tax owed when an heir receives the house?

No. Transfers by inheritance or devise are exempt under WAC 458-61A-202. A later sale by the heir to a buyer is taxable on the full sale price.

How soon must a will be filed after death?

A person holding the will must deliver it to the court or the named executor within thirty days of learning of the death, and an executor must deliver it to the court within forty days, under RCW 11.20.010.
